events.title: Early Austronesian Migration
events.description: Archaeological evidence suggests that around 3000 BCE, ancestors of the Austronesian peoples began migrating from Southeast Asia to Pacific islands. The Palau archipelago may have seen its first traces of human activity during this period, though the exact timing of settlement remains debated. These early migrants possessed advanced seafaring technology, using outrigger canoes and celestial navigation to traverse vast ocean expanses.

events.title: Formal Settlement of Palau
events.description: Around 1000 BCE, Micronesians from Southeast Asia formally settled the Palau islands, becoming the ancestors of modern Palauans. They brought unique cultures, languages, and social organization forms. Archaeological findings reveal pottery, stone tools, and shell implements from this period, demonstrating early settlers' lifestyle and technological sophistication. Palauan language belongs to the Micronesian branch of the Austronesian language family.

events.title: Stone Age Cultural Development
events.description: Palauan residents developed sophisticated stone-working techniques during this period, including stone anchors, axes, and mortars. Stone anchors excavated from archaeological sites indicate Palauans had mastered advanced seafaring techniques, capable of deep-sea fishing and inter-island navigation. Social organization began to grow complex, with early social stratification emerging.

events.title: Maturation of Pottery Making
events.description: Palauan residents began widespread pottery production and use during this period for storing food and water. Pottery decorative patterns display unique artistic styles and reflect cultural exchange with other Micronesian islands. Archaeologists have discovered pottery fragments from this period at multiple sites, evidencing technological progress and trade networks of the time.

events.title: Construction of Stone Platforms
events.description: Palauans began constructing complex stone platforms (Stonework Terraces), structures made of large stone blocks used as burial sites and ceremonial places. Stone platform construction demonstrates the society's emphasis on ancestor worship and further social stratification. These structures required substantial labor and organizational capacity, reflecting the society's organizational level.

events.title: Development of Shell Money System
events.description: Palauans developed a unique shell money system called 'Udoud.' These shell currencies were used not only for trade but also symbolized social status and power. Particularly precious shell money often had legendary stories and was passed down through generations. This monetary system facilitated inter-island trade and social interaction, becoming an important component of Palauan culture.

events.title: Establishment of Village Society
events.description: Palauan society formed clear village structures during this period. Each village was led by chiefs (Rubak) with strict social hierarchies. Villages formed complex relationship networks through marriage alliances, trade, and warfare. Village land and resources were communally owned by clans and allocated according to traditional rules. This social organization continued into modern times.

events.title: Establishment of Clan System
events.description: Palauan society formed a complex matrilineal clan system. Clans (Kebliil) became the basic units of Palauan society, with land, titles, and property passing through maternal lines. Each clan had its own land, titles, and traditional stories. Clan relationships were maintained through complex ceremonies and reciprocity systems, including gift-giving, mutual aid, and collective defense.

events.title: Construction of Bai Meeting Houses
events.description: Palauans began constructing traditional men's meeting houses called 'Bai.' Bai served as the political, social, and cultural center of villages, accessible only to men. Interior decorations featured exquisite wood carvings and murals depicting mythological legends, historical events, and moral lessons. Bai construction and maintenance required whole village participation, symbolizing community cohesion. These buildings showcased Palauans' excellent architectural skills and artistic creativity.

events.title: Trade Relations with Yap
events.description: Palau established important trade relations with neighboring Yap island. Palau's limestone was transported to Yap to make the famous stone money (Rai). In exchange, Yap exported shells, pottery, and other goods to Palau. This trade relationship promoted cultural exchange between the two regions and influenced Palau's social structure and economic development. Navigators needed to master complex navigation techniques to complete this dangerous sea journey.

events.title: Pinnacle of Traditional Navigation
events.description: Palauan navigators developed highly precise seafaring techniques during this period. They used stars, currents, wave patterns, and bird migration for navigation, capable of long-distance voyages without modern instruments. Palauan canoe-building technology also reached high levels, constructing large double-hulled outrigger canoes suitable for ocean voyaging. These techniques enabled Palauans to trade and culturally exchange with distant islands.

events.title: Flourishing of Oral Tradition
events.description: Palauan culture heavily relied on oral tradition to transmit history, mythology, and knowledge. Professional storytellers (Ngesngesll) held prestigious positions in communities, responsible for memorizing and recounting clan histories, creation myths, and moral stories. These stories provided not only entertainment but also taught social norms and values. Palauan language developed rich poetic and rhetorical forms used in formal occasions and ceremonies. Oral tradition's flourishing ensured cultural knowledge transmission across generations.

events.title: Warfare and Territorial Disputes
events.description: Palauan villages frequently engaged in warfare, competing for land, resources, and political influence. Warriors enjoyed high social status, with war skills and courage highly valued. Warfare typically involved raids and ambushes, using spears, clubs, and slings as weapons. Victorious villages would demand tribute or land cessions from the defeated. However, warfare was also constrained by complex rules and rituals to limit unnecessary violence.

events.title: Sorcery and Traditional Beliefs
events.description: Palauans developed complex belief systems, believing nature was filled with spiritual forces. Sorcerers (Rechuodel) could communicate with spirits, performing healing, divination, and curses. People believed ancestral spirits influenced the living, conducting regular sacrificial ceremonies. Certain locations were considered sacred, such as specific rocks, caves, and trees. Sorcery and ritual practices permeated all aspects of daily life, from agriculture to warfare, from birth to death.

events.title: Women's Status in Society
events.description: Despite Palauan society being matrilineal, women held important positions in certain aspects. Land and titles passed through maternal lines, with female chiefs (Rubak a rengdil) playing key roles in clan affairs. However, political and military matters were primarily controlled by men. Women played core roles in agriculture, handicrafts, and household management. They made traditional clothing, wove baskets and mats, and cared for children and elderly. Women's knowledge and skills were crucial to community survival.

events.title: First European Sightings
events.description: Spanish explorers may have first sighted the Palau islands in the early 16th century. It is believed Portuguese explorers or Spanish navigators might have passed near Palauan waters while sailing between the Philippines and Moluccas. However, these early contacts left no detailed records and did not lead to colonial activity. Palau remained isolated and unaffected by foreign influence.

events.title: Spanish Exploration Records
events.description: Spanish explorers may have recorded the Caroline Islands' location in more detail during this period, but Palau remained rarely visited. Spain claimed sovereignty over the entire Micronesian region, incorporating it into Spanish East Indies, but actual control was minimal. Palau's remote location, combined with dangerous coral reefs and unpredictable currents, made it difficult to approach.

events.title: Spanish Official Discovery of Caroline Islands
events.description: Spanish explorer Francisco Padilla officially recorded the discovery of the Caroline Islands, including Palau. Spain named these islands the Caroline Islands in honor of Spanish King Charles II. Despite official discovery records, Spain had almost no actual control or colonial activity over these islands for over a century. Palau continued its traditional way of life, undisturbed by foreign interference.

events.title: Captain Wilson's Shipwreck
events.description: The British East India Company merchant ship 'Antelope' ran aground on coral reefs near Koror, forcing Captain Henry Wilson and crew to stay in Palau for over three months. Wilson established friendly relations with Koror's high chief Ibedul. Palauans helped the British build a new ship; in return, Wilson showed them European tools and technology. This contact was the first recorded substantial interaction between Europe and Palau.

events.title: Prince Lebuu Travels to England
events.description: Lebuu, second son of Chief Ibedul, volunteered to accompany Captain Wilson to England, becoming the first Palauan to visit Europe. Lebuu was curious about the outside world, hoping to learn European knowledge and technology. However, Lebuu stayed in England only six months before dying of smallpox at about age 20. His death deeply saddened the British, and Wilson promised to visit Palau again. Lebuu's story became a symbol of Palau's contact with the West.

events.title: Publication of Wilson's Voyage Account
events.description: Captain Wilson's voyage account 'An Account of the Pelew Islands' was published in London, detailing Palau's society, culture, and natural environment. The book attracted widespread attention in Europe, making Palau known to the Western world for the first time. Wilson's relatively positive description of Palauans praised their honesty, friendliness, and social organization. The book sparked European interest in Pacific islands and led to more exploration activities.

events.title: British Expedition Revisits Palau
events.description: Britain dispatched an expedition to return to Palau, fulfilling Wilson's promise and further exploring the region. The expedition brought gifts and tools, meeting again with Chief Ibedul. However, this visit did not establish long-term connections, and Britain did not seek to colonize Palau. The expedition collected more information about Palau, including geography, flora and fauna, and anthropological data, enriching European knowledge of the Pacific.

events.title: Occasional Visits by Whaling Ships
events.description: In the early 19th century, increasing numbers of European and American whaling ships operated in the Pacific, with some vessels occasionally coming to Palauan waters seeking supplies and rest. These visits brought foreign goods such as metal tools, cloth, and firearms, beginning to change Palauan material culture. However, these contacts also brought diseases that severely impacted Palauans lacking immunity. Some crew members stayed in Palau, intermarrying with locals, becoming early cultural mixing phenomena.

events.title: British Explorer James Morrell Visits
events.description: British explorer James Morrell visited Palau conducting scientific surveys. He recorded Palau's geography, flora and fauna, and human society, providing more information about Palau to the West. Morrell's reports showed Palauan society still maintained its traditional way of life but had begun contacting foreign goods. He noted Palauans were particularly interested in metal tools, willing to exchange food and handicrafts.

events.title: First Christian Missionary Attempts
events.description: Catholic and Protestant missionaries began attempting to establish mission stations in Palau, but early efforts mostly failed. Palauans were cautious about foreign religions, preferring to maintain their traditional beliefs. Missionaries faced language barriers, disease, and cultural differences. However, these early contacts laid foundations for later religious spread. Some missionaries learned Palauan and began translating religious texts.

events.title: Increased Spanish Contact with Palau
events.description: Spain dispatched officials and missionaries from the Philippines to visit the Caroline Islands, including Palau, attempting to strengthen control over the region. Spain claimed historical sovereignty over these islands, but its actual presence remained limited. Spanish interest in Palau was primarily religious, hoping to convert locals to Catholicism. However, lack of resources and manpower limited Spanish colonial efforts.

events.title: British Merchant Andrew Cheyne's Activities
events.description: British merchant Andrew Cheyne began trading in Palau, purchasing copra, sea cucumbers, and shells. He established commercial relationships with local chiefs, bringing European goods to Palau, including tools, cloth, firearms, and alcohol. This trade accelerated changes in Palauan society, as traditional barter was gradually replaced by monetary economy. Cheyne's activities also attracted other European merchants' interest, and Palau began integrating into global trade networks.

events.title: Spanish-German Dispute
events.description: German merchants began operating in the Caroline Islands, conflicting with Spanish sovereignty claims. Germany believed that since Spain had not effectively occupied these islands, its sovereignty claims were invalid. This dispute reflected late 19th-century European powers' expansionist competition in the Pacific. German merchants established trading posts in Palau, purchasing copra and other products, with economic activities more vigorous than Spain's.

events.title: Caroline Islands Crisis
events.description: Germany attempted to occupy the Caroline Islands, raising the German flag on Yap island, triggering a diplomatic crisis with Spain known as the 'Caroline Islands Crisis.' Spain strongly protested, claiming historical sovereignty over these islands. The two countries nearly went to war, finally reaching an agreement through Pope Leo XIII's mediation. The Pope ruled that Spain had sovereignty, but Germany enjoyed trading and base establishment rights. This event marked Palau's formal entry into the colonial era.

events.title: Spain Formally Establishes Colonial Rule
events.description: After the Caroline Islands Crisis, Spain formally declared colonial rule over Palau and the Caroline Islands. Spain dispatched officials, soldiers, and Catholic missionaries to Palau, establishing an administrative center in Koror. Spanish rule focused on religious conversion and maintaining order, with limited interest in economic development. Spain introduced some modern administrative systems but largely preserved traditional chiefs' power.

events.title: Expansion of Catholic Missions
events.description: Spanish Capuchin missionaries began systematic missionary work in Palau. They built churches, schools, and clinics, attempting to convert Palauans to Catholicism. Missionaries learned Palauan, translated religious texts, and tried to understand local culture. Though some Palauans accepted baptism, traditional beliefs remained deeply rooted. Missionaries also provided medical services, earning trust from some locals.

events.title: Limited Development Under Spanish Rule
events.description: During Spanish rule, Palau's economic and infrastructure development was limited. The Spanish government lacked funds and manpower for large-scale development. Main activities focused on religious conversion and maintaining basic order. German merchants continued to dominate economic activities, purchasing copra and other tropical products. Palau's population declined during this period, mainly due to introduced diseases like smallpox, dysentery, and influenza that caused severe casualties among locals lacking immunity.

events.title: Impact of Spanish-American War
events.description: The Spanish-American War erupted, with Spain's defeat resulting in loss of the Philippines and most Pacific colonies. Spain was unable to continue ruling the Caroline Islands, including Palau. Spain began seeking to sell these islands to other powers. Germany expressed interest in purchasing these islands, hoping to expand its Pacific colonial empire. This event foreshadowed Palau's entry into a new colonial era.

events.title: Germany Purchases Palau
events.description: Under the German-Spanish Treaty, Spain sold the Caroline Islands, Mariana Islands (except Guam), and Palau to Germany for 25 million pesetas (about 17 million marks). Palau became part of German New Guinea, administered by German colonial companies. Germany planned large-scale development of Palau's economic resources, particularly copra and phosphates. This marked Palau's entry into the German colonial period, with economic development becoming the focus of rule.

events.title: Establishment of German Administrative System
events.description: Germany established an administrative center in Koror, dispatching colonial officials and technicians. Germany introduced modern administrative and legal systems, abolishing some traditional customs like inter-village warfare. German rule was more efficient than Spanish but also more authoritarian. German officials tried to understand and utilize traditional chief systems, appointing pro-German chiefs and weakening opposition forces. Germany also established police and court systems to maintain colonial order.

events.title: German Economic Development Plans
events.description: German colonial authorities began large-scale economic development plans. They established coconut plantations, forcing Palauans to plant cash crops. Germany introduced modern agricultural techniques and tools, increasing copra production. Germany also prospected for mineral resources, particularly phosphates and bauxite. These development activities brought economic growth but also destroyed traditional lifestyles and land use patterns. Many Palauans were forced to leave traditional lands, becoming plantation workers.

events.title: Infrastructure Construction
events.description: Germany constructed infrastructure in Palau, including roads, wharves, and warehouses. Koror developed into an important trading port, connecting German Micronesian islands. Germany also established postal and telegraph systems, improving communications. This infrastructure promoted economic development but primarily served the colonial economy, with limited direct benefits to Palauans. Germany also introduced some modern medical facilities, but these mainly served colonial officials and merchants.

events.title: Outbreak of World War I
events.description: World War I erupted, with Germany fighting Allied powers including Britain, France, and Russia. Japan, as Britain's ally, declared war on Germany. The Japanese navy moved swiftly to occupy German colonies in the Pacific, including Palau. In October 1914, the Japanese navy occupied Palau without resistance, ending German colonial rule. This marked Palau's entry into the Japanese rule period, which would last 30 years and profoundly impact Palauan society.

events.title: Japanese Occupation of Palau
events.description: The Japanese naval fleet arrived in Palau, occupying the islands without encountering resistance. Few German officials and merchants were expelled or detained, with the Japanese military government taking over administrative authority. Japan initially implemented military control, gradually establishing civilian government. Japan claimed occupation was temporary, but actually planned long-term rule. Palauans adopted a wait-and-see attitude toward new rulers, uncertain what Japanese rule would bring.

events.title: Early Japanese Rule Policies
events.description: Japan established early governance structures in Palau, setting up police, courts, and tax systems. Japan inherited German economic facilities, continuing copra production and trade. Japanese officials tried to understand local culture, learning Palauan and establishing relationships with traditional chiefs. Japanese rule was more systematic than German but initially relatively moderate. Japan began recording Palau's population, resources, and customs, preparing for future development. This period laid foundations for Japan's long-term rule.

events.title: League of Nations Mandate
events.description: After World War I, the League of Nations assigned former German Micronesian islands, including Palau, to Japan as a Class C mandate. This arrangement gave Japan de facto colonial power, but nominally Japan had to report to the League and promote local welfare. Japan established the South Seas Bureau in Palau as the administrative agency for ruling Micronesia, with headquarters in Koror. Japan began long-term and systematic colonial planning.

events.title: Massive Influx of Japanese Immigrants
events.description: The Japanese government encouraged Japanese civilians to migrate to Palau, providing land and economic opportunities. Thousands of Japanese immigrants, including fishermen, merchants, farmers, and laborers, came to Palau. By the 1930s, Japanese and other Asian immigrants (mainly Okinawans, Koreans, and Taiwanese) outnumbered indigenous Palauans. This demographic change profoundly altered Palau's social structure and culture. Japanese controlled the economy and politics, with Palauans becoming a minority in their own land.

events.title: Urbanization of Koror
events.description: Under Japanese rule, Koror rapidly developed into a modern city, becoming the largest and most prosperous city in the Micronesian region. Japan constructed modern buildings, shops, restaurants, banks, hospitals, and schools. Koror had electricity, running water, and sewage systems, facilities extremely rare among Pacific islands at the time. Koror's population reached tens of thousands, becoming the administrative and commercial center of the South Seas Bureau. However, this prosperity mainly benefited Japanese immigrants, with indigenous Palauans mostly marginalized.

events.title: Implementation of Japanese Education System
events.description: Japan established a comprehensive education system in Palau. All Palauan children were required to receive Japanese-style education, learning Japanese language, history, and culture. The Japanese government built elementary and vocational schools, but higher education opportunities were limited, mainly reserved for Japanese. Education aimed at assimilating Palauans, making them loyal Japanese subjects. Traditional Palauan language and culture were suppressed in schools, and many young people began speaking Japanese, gradually becoming estranged from traditional culture. This policy had lasting impacts on Palauan culture.

events.title: Hijikata Hisakatsu and Palauan Story Boards
events.description: Japanese anthropologist Hijikata Hisakatsu came to Palau for cultural research. He deeply entered Palauan villages, recording traditional customs, myths, and arts. Hijikata's most important contribution was inventing 'Palauan Story Boards' (Itabori). He taught Palauan artists to transfer mythical stories and historical legends traditionally painted on Bai interior walls onto wood boards through hand carving, facilitating preservation and dissemination. These story boards depicted creation myths, hero legends, and moral fables, becoming a unique Palauan art form and remaining important cultural souvenirs today.

events.title: Commercial Prosperity of Koror
events.description: By the late 1920s, Koror became a prosperous commercial center with hundreds of shops, restaurants, entertainment venues, and banks. Japanese merchants dominated the economy, Okinawans ran small shops and restaurants, and Koreans and Taiwanese performed labor work. Koror's streets were lively, with cinemas, dance halls, and bars. However, wealth distribution was unequal, with Japanese immigrants enjoying prosperity while indigenous Palauans mostly performed low-wage work or maintained traditional lifestyles. Social stratification was clear, with de facto racial segregation.

events.title: Impact of the Great Depression
events.description: The global Great Depression affected Palau, with copra and other export product prices plummeting and the economy falling into difficulty. The Japanese colonial government cut spending, with many development projects delayed or canceled. Unemployment rose and living standards declined. However, the Japanese government continued investing in military facilities due to Palau's increasingly important strategic position in the Pacific. Economic difficulties intensified social tensions, making relationships between Palauans and Japanese immigrants more strained.

events.title: Japan Withdraws from League of Nations
events.description: After being condemned by the League for aggression in Manchuria, Japan announced withdrawal from the League of Nations. This decision freed Japan from international oversight in Palau and other mandate territories. Japan began secretly constructing military bases in Palau, violating mandate terms. The Japanese military built airfields, fortresses, and naval bases in Palau, transforming it into an important stronghold in Pacific defenses. Foreigners were banned from entering these islands, and Palau became a military restricted zone.

events.title: Acceleration of Militarization
events.description: As Japanese militarism strengthened, Palau's militarization accelerated. Japan constructed extensive military facilities on Peleliu, Angaur, and main Palau islands, including airfields, gun batteries, air-raid shelters, and ammunition depots. Thousands of Japanese soldiers were stationed in Palau. Palauans were forcibly conscripted for military construction under harsh conditions with minimal wages. Military activities dominated Palau's economy, severely affecting civilian economy. Social atmosphere became oppressive and tense, preparing for the coming war.

events.title: Impact of Sino-Japanese War
events.description: After the Sino-Japanese War erupted, Japan further strengthened Palau's military defenses. More soldiers and supplies were transported to Palau, with military facilities continuing to expand. Wartime economic measures were implemented, supplies rationed, and public freedom further restricted. Palau became an important base for Japan's southward policy, supporting military operations in Southeast Asia and the Pacific. Palauan lives became more difficult, with traditional livelihood activities seriously disrupted.

events.title: Outbreak of Pacific War
events.description: Japan attacked Pearl Harbor, and the Pacific War erupted. Palau, as an important Japanese military base, became the front line. The Japanese navy and air force used Palau as a springboard to attack the Philippines, New Guinea, and Solomon Islands. Palau entered a wartime state, implementing strict military control. The populace was mobilized to support the war, with living conditions drastically deteriorating. Food and supplies were scarce, forcing people to grow food crops for self-sufficiency. Palauans felt fear and anxiety about the war, uncertain of the future.

events.title: U.S. Air Raids on Palau
events.description: As U.S. forces counterattacked in the Pacific, Palau became an important attack target. In March and April 1944, U.S. forces conducted massive air raids on Palau, attacking airfields, ports, and military facilities. Large numbers of Japanese ships and aircraft were destroyed, and Koror suffered severe damage. Japanese garrison forces suffered major losses but still resisted stubbornly. Japanese military command ordered civilian evacuation to remote islands and mountainous areas to avoid warfare. Many Palauans and Japanese civilians were killed or injured in air raids.

events.title: Battle of Peleliu Begins
events.description: The U.S. 1st Marine Division landed on Peleliu Island, beginning one of the bloodiest battles in the Pacific War. U.S. forces originally expected to capture the island within days but encountered stubborn resistance from Japanese defenders. Japanese commander Colonel Kunio Nakagawa adopted new defensive tactics, using island caves and bunkers for protracted warfare. Fighting proceeded in sweltering conditions with heavy casualties on both sides. The battle's ferocity shocked U.S. forces and changed Pacific War tactics.

events.title: Battle of Peleliu Ends
events.description: After over two months of intense combat, the Battle of Peleliu finally ended. U.S. forces paid the price of about 2,300 killed and over 8,000 wounded to capture this small island. Japanese defenders numbered over 10,000, with almost all killed and only a few captured. The battle's strategic value was later questioned, as U.S. forces could have bypassed Palau to continue toward the Philippines. Peleliu became one of the Pacific War's most brutal battlefields, with war relics still visible today, including bunkers and tank remains.

events.title: Battle of Angaur
events.description: Simultaneously with the Battle of Peleliu, the U.S. 81st Infantry Division landed on Angaur Island. This battle was relatively short but equally bloody. Japanese defenders numbered about 1,400, almost all killed, with U.S. casualties about 260 killed and over 1,300 wounded. Angaur's capture provided U.S. forces an important airfield to support attacks on the Philippines. After the war, Angaur's war relics became historical testimony, attracting visitors.

events.title: Japanese Surrender and War's End
events.description: On August 15, 1945, Japan announced unconditional surrender, ending World War II. Japanese defenders in Palau ceased resistance, surrendering to U.S. forces. The war caused tremendous destruction to Palau: cities destroyed, infrastructure paralyzed, population greatly reduced. Many Japanese civilians and Palauans died during the war. Surviving Japanese civilians and soldiers were repatriated to Japan, ending over 30 years of Japanese rule. Palau entered the American administration period, beginning the long process of reconstruction and recovery.

events.title: U.S. Military Government Rule
events.description: After the war, the U.S. Navy established a military government administering Palau and other former Japanese mandate territories. The U.S. military's priority was clearing war debris, restoring basic order, and providing humanitarian aid. Palau's population was greatly reduced during the war, with survivors facing hunger, disease, and housing shortages. U.S. forces provided food, medical care, and housing assistance, helping Palauans rebuild their lives. The military government also began clearing unexploded ordnance left from the war, work continuing for years.

events.title: UN Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands
events.description: The UN Security Council passed a resolution establishing former Japanese mandate Micronesian islands, including Palau, Marshall Islands, Federated States of Micronesia, and Northern Mariana Islands, as the 'Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands' administered by the United States. This was the UN's only strategic trusteeship, granting the U.S. rights to establish military bases in the region. The U.S. promised to promote local self-government and development, but actually mainly focused on strategic interests.

events.title: Beginning of Civilian Administration
events.description: The U.S. transferred trust territory administration from the Navy to the Department of Interior, ending military government rule and beginning civilian administration. The Interior Department established the Government of the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands, with headquarters initially in Guam, later moved to Saipan. The U.S. began establishing education, healthcare, and infrastructure systems, but investment was relatively limited. Palauans began receiving American-style education, learning English. The traditional chief system was partially restored but had limited power, mainly symbolic.

events.title: Strategic Value in Cold War Context
events.description: In the Cold War context, Palau and other Micronesian islands' strategic value increased. The U.S. maintained military presence in the region, monitoring Soviet and Chinese activities in the Pacific. The U.S. conducted nuclear tests in the Marshall Islands; though Palau was not directly affected by nuclear testing, regional militarization raised concerns among locals. The U.S. government's investment in trust territories' economic and social development was limited, mainly focusing on strategic interests, leading to local economic stagnation.

events.title: First Elections
events.description: The U.S. held the first local elections in the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands, with Palauans beginning to elect local council representatives. Though power was limited, this was the first time Palauans participated in politics through democratic procedures. Power relationships between traditional chiefs and emerging elected leaders began changing. Young, American-educated Palauans began entering the political arena, challenging traditional authority. This marked the beginning of Palauan political modernization but also caused tensions between tradition and modernity.

events.title: Expansion of Education System
events.description: The U.S. expanded the education system in Palau, building more schools and providing scholarships for Palauan students to receive higher education in Guam, Hawaii, and the U.S. mainland. English became the language of instruction, replacing Japanese. A new generation of Palauans received Western-style education, beginning to form modern political and social consciousness. However, educational Westernization also led young people to become estranged from traditional culture and language. Many Palauans with higher education chose to remain in the U.S., causing brain drain.

events.title: Discussion of Future Political Status Referendum
events.description: The Congress of Micronesia began seriously discussing future political status options. Palauan representatives proposed various plans, including complete independence, free association, becoming a U.S. territory, or incorporation into the U.S. Palau internally divided on these options, reflecting different interest groups' demands. Some wanted complete independence, preserving sovereignty and culture; others wanted close ties with the U.S. for economic benefits. This discussion laid groundwork for over a decade of political struggle.

events.title: Micronesian Political Status Commission
events.description: The Micronesian Political Status Commission conducted multiple rounds of negotiations with the U.S., discussing the trust territory's future. The U.S. mainly focused on retaining military rights, including base establishment, sea usage, and strategic denial rights. Micronesian representatives demanded more autonomy and economic aid. Negotiations were slow and complex, with different island groups having different interests, making unified positions difficult. Palauan representatives insisted on environmental protection clauses, laying groundwork for the later nuclear-free constitution.

events.title: First Compact of Free Association Referendum
events.description: In February 1983, Palau held the first referendum on the Compact of Free Association. The referendum required 75% support to amend the constitution's nuclear-free clause. Results showed 61% support, failing to reach the threshold. Opposition consisted of environmental activists and traditional leaders insisting Palau should maintain nuclear-free status. Supporters argued the compact was crucial for economic development. The referendum's failure marked the beginning of a decade-long political deadlock, deeply dividing Palauan society.

events.title: Rise of Environmental Protection Movement
events.description: In the early 1990s, Palau's environmental awareness began awakening. Environmental activists warned of threats from overfishing, coral reef destruction, and pollution. Palauans recognized that clean environment and rich marine resources were foundations for their future economic development. Some communities began voluntarily establishing marine protected areas, limiting fishing and protecting coral reefs. This movement laid foundations for Palau becoming a global environmental leader, reflecting the combination of traditional resource management wisdom and modern environmental concepts.

events.title: First Presidential Election
events.description: The first presidential election after independence was held in 1996, with Kuniwo Nakamura successfully reelected, demonstrating Palauan democratic system stability. The election process was peaceful and orderly with high voter turnout, showing Palauan enthusiasm for democratic politics. The Nakamura government focused on economic development, infrastructure construction, and international relations expansion. However, Palau still faced economic difficulties, highly dependent on U.S. aid. The government began seeking diversified aid sources and investment opportunities.

events.title: Beginning of Diving Tourism Development
events.description: In the late 1990s, Palau began being 'discovered' by the international diving community, praised as one of the world's top diving destinations. Palau has over 700 coral species and 1,400 fish species, with dive sites like Blue Corner, Blue Hole, and German Channel world-famous. The government began consciously developing diving tourism, establishing dive centers, training dive guides, and setting safety standards. Jellyfish Lake became a unique tourist attraction, attracting many visitors. Diving tourism brought important income to Palau but also raised environmental protection concerns.

events.title: Rock Islands Listed on World Heritage Tentative List
events.description: Palau began applying to list the Rock Islands on UNESCO's World Heritage List. The Rock Islands consist of hundreds of mushroom-shaped limestone islands with unique landscapes, rich ecology, marine lakes, coral reefs, and abundant biodiversity. The area also has important archaeological sites, including ancient villages and burial sites. The application process required strengthening protection measures and management planning. This effort reflected Palau's commitment to protecting natural and cultural heritage.

events.title: Rapid Growth of Tourism Industry
events.description: In the early 2010s, Palau's tourism industry entered a rapid growth period, with annual visitors increasing from tens of thousands to over 100,000. Main visitors came from Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and mainland China. Tourism became Palau's largest industry, creating many job opportunities. However, rapid growth also brought challenges: environmental pressure, insufficient infrastructure, excessive Jellyfish Lake visitors causing jellyfish population decline. The Palauan government began recognizing the need to balance tourism development with environmental protection, exploring sustainable tourism models.

events.title: Rock Islands Southern Lagoon Listed as World Heritage
events.description: In 2012, UNESCO officially listed the 'Rock Islands Southern Lagoon' on the World Heritage List, recognizing its outstanding natural beauty and biodiversity. This was Palau's first World Heritage site and Micronesia's first mixed heritage (natural and cultural). World Heritage status elevated Palau's international profile, attracting more visitors but also requiring Palau to fulfill stricter protection obligations. The Palauan government strengthened protected area management, limiting development activities to ensure heritage site integrity.

events.title: 20th Anniversary of Palau Independence
events.description: On October 1, 2014, Palau celebrated 20 years of independence. Over the past 20 years, Palau made significant progress in democratic governance, economic development, and environmental protection. Palau successfully established a stable democratic system, achieving peaceful power transitions. Tourism flourished, becoming an economic pillar. Palau's leadership position in marine protection received international recognition. However, Palau still faced challenges: economic overdependence on tourism and aid, brain drain, aging infrastructure, and climate change threats. Celebration activities included cultural performances, sports competitions, and international conferences.

events.title: Peak of Chinese Tourist Wave
events.description: In 2016, Chinese tourist numbers reached their peak at over 90,000, accounting for more than half of Palau's total visitors. Chinese travel agencies chartered direct flights to Palau, bringing large tourist groups. This brought economic prosperity but also raised problems: increased environmental pressure, local service industry struggling to cope, some tourists behaving inappropriately. Palauan society had complex feelings about Chinese tourist influx, welcoming income but worrying about environment. After the 2017 Chinese tourism ban, Chinese tourists drastically decreased, severely impacting Palau's economy but relieving environmental pressure.

events.title: Sunscreen Ban Implementation Preparation
events.description: In 2019, Palau prepared for the 2020 sunscreen ban implementation. The government conducted publicity campaigns educating visitors and locals about reef-safe sunscreen products. Customs trained officials to inspect arriving passengers' luggage, confiscating prohibited sunscreens. Retailers cleared inventory, introducing compliant products. This law attracted international media attention, with many environmental organizations praising Palau's courage. Some tourists and businesses initially complained of inconvenience, but most understood this was a necessary measure to protect Palau's coral reefs.

events.title: Emergence of Self-Governance Awareness
events.description: In the 1960s, residents of Palau and other trust territories began demanding more autonomy. The younger generation, having received American education and learned more about democracy and human rights, began questioning American rule. Palauans demanded more representation in government and participation in decision-making processes. Under UN pressure, the U.S. began considering granting trust territories more autonomy, but progress was slow. This period also saw discussions about future political status—independence, incorporation into the U.S., or maintaining special relationship with the U.S.

events.title: Congress of Micronesia Established
events.description: The U.S. established the Congress of Micronesia as the legislative body of the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. This was the first opportunity for locals to participate in government through elected representatives. The Congress consisted of representatives from Palau, Federated States of Micronesia, Marshall Islands, and Northern Mariana Islands. Though the Congress had limited power, mainly advisory, it provided a platform for local political elites to discuss future political status. The Congress quickly became an important force pushing for self-governance and independence.

events.title: Future Political Status Negotiations Begin
events.description: The Congress of Micronesia established a Future Political Status Commission, beginning formal negotiations with the U.S. government. The Commission proposed multiple options, including complete independence, free association, and incorporation into the U.S. The negotiation process was complex and lengthy because different island groups had different interests and wishes. Palau leaned toward free association, maintaining economic and defense ties with the U.S. while gaining domestic autonomy. However, the U.S. mainly focused on military base rights and strategic control, with both sides disagreeing on key issues.

events.title: Micronesian Federation Referendum and Palau's Separation
events.description: In 1978, Micronesia held a referendum to decide whether to form a unified Federated States of Micronesia. Palauans voted against joining the federation, choosing to negotiate separately with the U.S. The Marshall Islands and Northern Mariana Islands also chose separation. Only Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei, and Kosrae chose to form the Federated States of Micronesia. Palau decided to pursue its own path to independence, believing this would better protect its interests and culture. This decision marked a critical step in Palau's journey toward independence.

events.title: Palau Constitution Referendum
events.description: In 1979, Palau held a referendum adopting its own constitution. The Palauan constitution established a democratic republic, including a presidential system, bicameral legislature (Senate and House of Delegates), and independent judicial system. The constitution also included a unique and controversial clause: prohibiting the storage, testing, or disposal of nuclear, biological, or chemical weapons on Palauan territory. This 'nuclear-free clause' reflected Palauan commitment to peace but also became a major obstacle in negotiating the Compact of Free Association with the U.S., as the U.S. wanted to retain rights to deploy nuclear weapons in Palau.

events.title: Republic of Palau Established
events.description: On January 1, 1981, the Republic of Palau was formally established, with Haruo Remeliik elected as the first president. Palau began self-government operations but remained under U.S. trusteeship, not yet fully independent. The new government faced many challenges, including establishing effective administrative systems, developing the economy, and negotiating the Compact of Free Association with the U.S. President Remeliik was committed to promoting Palau's modernization and independence process but also faced domestic political divisions and economic difficulties.

events.title: Repeated Compact of Free Association Referendums
events.description: Palau and the U.S. signed the Compact of Free Association, but the compact required amending the constitution's nuclear-free clause, thus needing 75% voter support to pass. From 1982 to 1992, Palau held up to 7 referendums attempting to approve the compact, but each time failed to reach the 75% threshold. This long and painful process reflected profound divisions in Palauan society: some wanted to maintain close ties with the U.S. for economic aid, while others insisted on nuclear-free principles. The referendum process was accompanied by intense political struggles and social conflicts.

events.title: Assassination of President Remeliik
events.description: On June 30, 1985, Palau's first president Haruo Remeliik was shot to death at his home, shocking the entire nation. This assassination remains unsolved, but is widely believed related to political struggles over the Compact of Free Association. Remeliik's death marked Palau's entry into a turbulent political period, with violence and intimidation becoming means of political struggle. This event exposed the fragility of small island nation politics and reflected profound contradictions and conflicts of interest in the independence process.

events.title: President Lazarus Salii's Suicide
events.description: On August 20, 1987, Palauan President Lazarus Salii shot himself at home; officially ruled suicide, though some suspected foul play. President Salii was a Compact of Free Association supporter, and his death further deepened Palau's political crisis. The abnormal deaths of two consecutive presidents plunged Palau into political chaos, with international society expressing concern about Palau's political stability. These tragic events highlighted the difficulty and complexity of Palau's independence process.

events.title: Modification of Nuclear-Free Clause Threshold
events.description: After multiple failed referendums, the Palauan government decided to amend the constitution, lowering the support required to approve the Compact of Free Association from 75% to a simple majority (over 50%). This amendment itself required referendum approval and was passed in November 1992. This decision was controversial; opponents argued it violated the constitution's spirit and was a compromise under U.S. pressure. However, supporters believed it was a necessary step toward independence, as Palau needed U.S. economic support to survive.

events.title: Final Approval of Compact of Free Association
events.description: In November 1993, Palau held its eighth referendum, this time requiring only a simple majority to approve the Compact of Free Association. The referendum passed with 68% support, ending over a decade of political deadlock. The compact stipulated that the U.S. would provide $450 million in economic aid over 15 years, and in exchange, the U.S. gained Palau's defense responsibility and military usage rights. Palau agreed to allow U.S. naval vessels (including nuclear-powered ships) to enter its waters. The compact's approval paved the way for Palau's independence.

events.title: Palau Formal Independence
events.description: On October 1, 1994, Palau formally gained independence, becoming the world's 185th independent nation and the last to emerge from UN trusteeship. The Compact of Free Association officially took effect, establishing a special relationship between Palau and the U.S. Palauan President Kuniwo Nakamura presided over independence celebrations, attended by the UN Secretary-General and representatives from many nations. Palau's independence marked completion of Pacific island decolonization and opened a new chapter in Palauan history. As a small but beautiful island nation, Palau faced challenges of nation-building, economic development, and sovereignty maintenance.

events.title: Joining the United Nations
events.description: On December 15, 1994, Palau officially joined the United Nations, becoming the 185th member state. This marked Palau's full recognition by the international community, able to voice concerns on the world stage. Palau actively participated in UN affairs, particularly focusing on climate change, ocean protection, and small island states' rights. As a UN member, Palau established diplomatic relations with countries worldwide, seeking international cooperation and aid. Palauan UN representatives often advocated for Pacific island nations' interests, opposing nuclear testing and environmental destruction.

events.title: Economic Development and Tourism Beginning
events.description: After independence, Palau began developing its economy, with tourism identified as an economic pillar. Palau possessed world-class diving sites, beautiful Jellyfish Lake, and rich marine life, attracting international tourists. The government invested in improving airports, hotels, and tourism infrastructure. However, the Palauan economy was highly dependent on U.S. aid, with slow local industry development. Fisheries and agriculture remained traditional livelihoods but on a limited scale. Palau faced challenges of economic diversification, seeking to balance tourism development with environmental protection.

events.title: Establishment of Diplomatic Relations with ROC
events.description: On December 29, 1999, Palau established formal diplomatic relations with the Republic of China (Taiwan), with embassies set up in each other's capitals. Taiwan became an important source of aid and investment for Palau, providing economic assistance, technical support, and scholarships. The two countries cooperated in agriculture, fisheries, healthcare, and education. Palau supported Taiwan's participation in international organizations on international occasions. This diplomatic relationship embroiled Palau in the complex cross-strait situation, facing pressure from mainland China, but the Palauan government insisted on friendship with Taiwan, believing it served Palau's interests.

events.title: Strengthened Environmental Protection Awareness
events.description: Palau began strengthening environmental protection, recognizing that a clean environment was the foundation of tourism. The government formulated policies for marine protected areas, limiting fishing and protecting coral reefs. Palauans traditionally lived in harmony with nature, and modern environmental movements continued this tradition. Palau became an environmental pioneer in the Pacific region, with its experiences learned by other island nations. However, balancing environmental protection with economic development remained challenging, especially facing pressures from rapid tourism growth.

events.title: Tommy Remengesau Elected President
events.description: In 2001, Tommy Remengesau Jr. was elected Palauan President, beginning his first term (2001-2009). Remengesau was a reform leader committed to environmental protection, tourism development, and government modernization. He promoted multiple environmental protection laws, enhancing Palau's international image. Remengesau's leadership brought Palau a relatively stable and prosperous period. He was reelected in 2013, serving until 2021, becoming one of Palau's most influential leaders.

events.title: Capital Relocation to Ngerulmud
events.description: On October 7, 2006, Palau relocated its capital from Koror to Ngerulmud on Babeldaob island. The new Capitol Building was completed in 2006, modeled after the U.S. Capitol, becoming Palau's iconic building. Relocation aimed to disperse population, promote Babeldaob development, and relieve pressure on Koror. However, Ngerulmud remained a small administrative center, with most commercial and economic activities still concentrated in Koror. The Capitol Building's construction cost sparked some controversy, with critics calling it too extravagant for a small nation.

events.title: Establishment of Shark Sanctuary
events.description: In 2009, Palau announced establishment of the world's first shark sanctuary in its entire exclusive economic zone (about 600,000 square kilometers), completely prohibiting commercial shark fishing. This pioneering measure earned praise from international environmental organizations, making Palau a global leader in ocean protection. Sharks are crucial to coral reef ecosystems and a major attraction for Palau's diving tourism. The shark sanctuary's establishment reflected Palau's determination to prioritize environmental protection over economic interests, setting an example for other nations.

events.title: Launch of the Palau Pledge
events.description: The Palauan government introduced the 'Palau Pledge,' requiring all entering visitors to sign an environmental commitment on their passports, promising to protect Palau's environment and culture, not harm marine life, and not damage coral reefs. This innovative measure extended environmental responsibility to visitors, making each visitor a participant in environmental protection. The Palau Pledge became a global first, receiving widespread international media coverage and enhancing Palau's image as a responsible tourism destination. The pledge content was written by Palauan children, reflecting responsibility to future generations.

events.title: Palau National Marine Sanctuary
events.description: In 2015, President Remengesau signed the Palau National Marine Sanctuary Act, designating 80% of the exclusive economic zone (about 500,000 square kilometers) as a fully no-take marine reserve, becoming one of the world's largest marine protected areas. The remaining 20% of waters were reserved for local fishers for traditional fishing and limited commercial fishing. This bold move sacrificed short-term fishery income to protect long-term ocean ecosystem health. International environmental organizations praised Palau's courage and vision, with Palau again demonstrating small nation leadership in environmental protection.

events.title: Chinese Tourism Ban
events.description: In 2017, mainland China's government imposed an unofficial tourism ban on Palau, restricting Chinese travel agencies from organizing tour groups to Palau as punishment for Palau maintaining diplomatic relations with Taiwan. Previously, Chinese tourist numbers had surged, once accounting for over half of Palau's visitors. The tourism ban dealt a major blow to Palau's tourism industry, severely affecting hotels, aviation, and tourism-related businesses. However, the Palauan government insisted on maintaining diplomatic relations with Taiwan, refusing to yield to pressure. This incident highlighted small nations' vulnerability in great power geopolitical competition and tested Palau's diplomatic resilience.

events.title: Sunscreen Ban Law
events.description: In 2018, Palau passed the world's first law banning reef-toxic sunscreen, taking effect in 2020. The law prohibited import or sale of sunscreen products containing 10 chemical ingredients including oxybenzone and octinoxate, with violators fined. These chemicals were scientifically proven to damage coral reefs, causing bleaching and death. Palau again pioneered environmental protection, with many countries and regions subsequently following suit. This law reflected Palau's firm commitment to coral reef protection, as coral reefs are foundations of Palau's ecology and economy.

events.title: Pandemic Impact and Travel Bubble
events.description: In 2020, the COVID-19 pandemic erupted, with Palau closing borders and tourism completely halting. The Palauan economy was highly dependent on tourism, with the pandemic causing serious economic difficulties, rising unemployment, and business closures. However, due to strict border controls, Palau successfully avoided community transmission, becoming one of few zero-case nations. To restart the economy, Palau negotiated with Taiwan, also controlling the pandemic well, to establish a 'travel bubble,' allowing travelers from both countries to visit without quarantine. This innovative measure provided economic and psychological relief for both countries during the pandemic.

events.title: Surangel Whipps Jr. Elected President
events.description: In January 2021, Surangel Whipps Jr. was inaugurated as Palauan President, succeeding Remengesau. Whipps was a Palauan business leader, promising to promote economic recovery, infrastructure construction, and tourism diversification. He continued predecessor environmental policies while seeking to attract more investment and develop new industries. Whipps firmly supported diplomatic relations with Taiwan, visiting Taiwan multiple times to strengthen cooperation. His inauguration marked smooth political power transition in Palau, demonstrating democratic system maturity.

events.title: Palau-Taiwan Travel Bubble Launch
events.description: On March 28, 2021, President Whipps visited Taiwan, officially launching the 'travel bubble' plan between the two countries. This was the world's first international travel bubble, allowing travelers from both countries to visit without quarantine under specific conditions. The first Taiwanese tour groups arrived in Palau on April 1, receiving warm welcomes. The travel bubble brought much-needed income to Palau's tourism industry and demonstrated close ties between the two countries. However, due to pandemic changes in Taiwan, the travel bubble was suspended in May, but this attempt still had important symbolic and practical significance.

events.title: Climate Change Threats
events.description: As a low-elevation island nation, Palau faced severe threats from climate change, including sea level rise, coral bleaching, extreme weather, and ocean acidification. In 2021, the Palauan president addressed the UN climate summit, calling for urgent global action to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Palau emphasized that for small island nations, climate change was not a distant future threat but a present survival crisis. Though Palau's own emissions were negligible, it suffered disproportionate impacts. Palau called on developed countries to fulfill climate financing commitments, helping vulnerable nations adapt to climate change.

events.title: Deepening U.S.-Palau Relations
events.description: In 2022, the U.S. and Palau began negotiating renewal of the Compact of Free Association, set to expire in 2024. The U.S. recognized Palau's importance in Indo-Pacific strategy, especially in countering China's expanding influence. The U.S. promised increased economic aid and infrastructure improvements, including repairing Babeldaob roads. The U.S. also provided security and law enforcement support, helping Palau combat illegal fishing and maintain maritime sovereignty. Strengthened U.S.-Palau relations reflected changing geopolitical landscape, with Palau's strategic value rising in great power competition.

events.title: Tourism Recovery and Challenges
events.description: In 2023, as the global pandemic eased, Palau reopened borders with tourism gradually recovering. However, recovery was slower than expected, mainly due to absent Chinese tourists and reduced international flights. The Palauan government worked to attract visitors from Japan, Korea, the U.S., and Europe, promoting high-end, sustainable tourism. Palau's challenge was finding balance between increasing visitor numbers and protecting environment. Overtourism could destroy Palau's natural beauty on which it depended, so Palau emphasized quality over quantity, attracting environmentally respectful responsible tourists.

events.title: Compact of Free Association Renewal
events.description: In 2024, the U.S. and Palau completed negotiating renewal of the Compact of Free Association. The new compact extended U.S. economic aid and defense commitments to Palau, with significantly increased aid amounts to address inflation and Palau's development needs. The U.S. promised investment in Palau's infrastructure, education, healthcare, and climate adaptation capacity. In exchange, the U.S. continued to enjoy Palau's defense responsibility and strategic denial rights, able to reject other nations establishing military presence in Palau. The compact's renewal ensured Palau's economic stability and security guarantees but also meant Palau remained influenced by the U.S. in foreign and security policies.

events.title: Palau's Current Status and Future
events.description: In 2024, Palau is a small island nation with a population of about 18,000, possessing unique culture, magnificent natural beauty, and strong environmental consciousness. Palau's economy mainly depends on tourism, U.S. aid, and fisheries. Palau is internationally renowned as an environmental protection leader, with its marine protected areas and environmental policies becoming global models. Palau faces multiple challenges: survival threats from climate change, need for economic diversification, brain drain, insufficient infrastructure, and geopolitical pressures. Palau maintains firm diplomatic relations with Taiwan, resisting Chinese pressure. Palau's future depends on finding balance between environmental protection and economic development, maintaining independence while accepting aid, and safeguarding its interests in great power competition. As a pearl of the Pacific, Palau demonstrates that small nations can exert tremendous influence in environmental and diplomatic spheres, with its experiences and persistence providing valuable insights to the world.
